_meta.notes: Schema v3: items split into 'vehicle' and 'equipment' groups via the `group` field on each entry. Per-item `maintenance` block added with at-a-store reference for fuel, oil, sparkPlug, filters, consumables. Confidence convention: each maintenance value tagged 'verified' (manufacturer spec / OEM doc / on-unit sticker), 'inferred' (typical for product line — double-check before ordering), or 'tbd'.

vehicles.name: 2016 VW GTI

fuel.value: 91+ octane premium unleaded REQUIRED (APR Stage 1 needs 91-93 octane). Top Tier preferred.

oil.value: 5W-40 meeting VW 502.00 spec (e.g. Liqui Moly Top Tec 4200, Castrol Edge Pro). Capacity 5.3 qt (5L) with filter.

cabinFilter.value: VW OEM 5Q0 819 644 A (combination filter w/ activated carbon)

sparkPlugs.value: NGK PFR7S8EG — gap 0.028" (factory; tuned cars sometimes drop to 0.024–0.026"). Replace every 40k mi on Stage 1.

coolant.value: VW G13 (pink) — never mix with G11 or G12. Active leak under diagnosis: check thermostat housing + expansion tank cap first.

transmissionFluid.value: DSG service fluid VW G 052 182 A2 — service every 40k mi

vehicles.notes: APR Stage 1 software tune on stock hardware. Coolant leak source under investigation.

restoration.item: Coolant leak — water pump & thermostat housing
restoration.detail: Taking it in for diagnosis. This is the EA888 Gen 3's signature failure — the plastic water pump + thermostat housing assembly leaks at the seals. Ask the shop to confirm and quote the combined job, and to fit an upgraded metal-impeller water pump (INA/OEM kit) instead of another plastic one — same labor, longer life. Brace for ~$1.5–2k at a dealer; a good indie is less.
Fluid + filter. Interval is 40k / 80k miles — at ~90k it's past due. The highest-value 'while it's in the shop' item; don't skip it. Spec: VW G 052 182 A2.
Time-based — every 2 years. Confirm when it was last done; if you can't remember, it's due. DOT 4 LV (VW G 060 157).
NGK PFR7S8EG, gap ~0.028" — replace every 40k on the Stage 1 tune. Likely due around now depending on the last change.
Engine air filter is due at 60k / 6 yr — almost certainly due. Swap the cabin filter while it's apart.
Direct injection builds carbon on the intake valves; 80–100k is the window to inspect and walnut-blast. Have the shop scope it and tell you how bad it is before you commit to the job.
No fixed interval; stretch usually needs action at 120–150k. A quick VCDS / OBDeleven read now gives a baseline — worth it on a tuned car.
Both are common softening/failure points on tuned MK7s. Cheap to inspect while it's at this visit.

vehicles.notes: "Bolores" — the Eddie Bauer edition: two-tone maroon over tan, upgraded interior. Lifted and riding on 35" Pro Comp mud-terrains over 15" alloys with WARN locking hubs; Mickey Thompson Baja spare on the rear carrier. Full restoration underway.

restoration.detail: 5 qt 5W-30 + Motorcraft FL-1A — see the maintenance reference above. ~30-minute job on shelf parts. Engine protection doesn't wait on the cosmetics, so it's first.
Drain, flush, refill with green 50/50 IAT (era-correct) — see the maintenance reference. A free-afternoon job; not urgent unless it comes out rusty.

Actuator already replaced with no fix, so the signal isn't reaching it. Next: meter power switch → actuator. Prime suspect is the door-jamb boot wiring (flexes and cracks inside the rubber boot where you can't see it); also check the switch and its ground. Same teardown as the door panel — do them together.

Buttons work; the plastic screw bosses (mount points) snapped off over time. Structural plastic repair — rebuild the bosses with Plastex or epoxy and re-drill pilots. No color match, nothing to source. The quick win you can do this week.

Chestnut plastic, cracked through — likely a replace, not a repair. Hunt an '87–91 Bronco/F-series panel (color match is the hard part). Long lead, so start the hunt now. Gates the audio build — a loose panel rattles and ruins subs. Same teardown as the lock.
Front driver seat needs an upholstery repair — find a local auto-upholstery / trim shop and get a quote. Match the chestnut interior.
Failing clear coat — outsource to a body shop. Get 2–3 quotes; scheduling has a long lead, so start the calls early even though the work lands later.
Replacement headliner — down the road. Common to re-do with the rest of the interior; can pair with the upholstery shop visit.
Sound-deadening (floors, doors, roof) — long-term comfort upgrade. Best done with panels off, so it pairs naturally with the door-panel and headliner work.
The audio build — farthest out, and deliberately last. Blocked until the door panels are solid: a rattling panel kills the point of a sub. Soundproofing first makes it sing.

vehicles.notes: Lightweight trail/dual-sport — good for property access and dirt roads. Fuel-efficient, easy to maintain. Recommissioned ~June 2026 after sitting: the tank and carb had been drained and the battery stored off the bike. Charged the battery, filled with ethanol-free gas, primed the carb, reconnected — fired right up nicely. Oil change still pending.

restoration.detail: First oil after sitting — not done since recommissioning. 10W-40 motorcycle-specific (JASO MA/MA2), ~1.0 qt with filter; filter Suzuki 16510-37450 / HiFlo HF138 (see maintenance). Do it now that she's running again.

Bars are bent. Recommendation: replace, don't re-straighten. The DR200S uses 7/8" (22 mm) bars; stock are steel, which can technically take one mild straightening — but a re-bent bar is permanently weakened, steel bars have been known to snap later, and the bar is a safety-critical control that's cheap to swap (~$30–45). Straighten only as a temporary trail-side fix on a mild steel bend; never re-straighten aluminum. Buy a 7/8" replacement (e.g. Renthal Rider 7/8", or an OEM-style steel bar) — pick the bend/pullback to taste.

vehicles.notes: Dual-sport — street-legal with headlight, tail light, and mirrors. VIN position 10 = '1' confirms 2001 model year. Recommissioned ~June 2026 the same way as the DR200: ethanol-free gas in, primed the carb, fully charged battery back on — fired right up. On the first test ride it developed an electrical fault (see the list).

restoration.item: Electrical fault — total power loss when steering
restoration.detail: Symptom (first test ride, June 2026): leaned the bike and turned the bars and ALL power died at once — headlight cut out instantly, then no response to the ignition on/off. KEY CONTEXT: the speedometer was already removed and its connectors taped off during this ride, so a speedo short is RULED OUT as the cause — the fault happened with it disconnected. But the same water that killed the speedo (see Speedometer item) likely reached nearby connectors, so it pushes the corrosion suspects below UP the list. Total power loss + dead headlight = a main power-feed interruption (battery feed, main ground, or the ignition-switch main circuit), not the engine-kill circuit. Trigger being handlebar movement points to a connection that flexes with steering. The carbureted DR-Z400S has no tip-over/lean sensor, so the lean itself didn't cut it — the wiring moved. Suspects, cheapest-first (water history weights the corroded ones): (1) Battery terminals + main ground to frame/engine — loose/corroded after sitting; a corroded connector behind the battery is a known DRZ cause of sudden death. Clean + torque first. (2) Ignition switch + its connector near the steering head — corroded (prime suspect given the water) and it flexes when you turn the bars: best match for 'died when I turned the bars.' (3) Main harness pinched/chafed at the steering head — wires get pinched between frame turn-stops and triple clamps (worse with risers); turn the bars lock-to-lock with the cowl off and watch. (4) Main fuse + fuse holder — corroded holder drops all power with vibration. Diagnose: key + headlight ON, wiggle the ignition connector and flex the harness at the steering head while watching the light — wherever it flickers/dies is the fault. Cross-check the horn + brake light (same feed) — if dead too, the fault is upstream in the power feed. Keep the taped speedo leads fully isolated so they can't short against the frame while you flex the harness.

Water got into the speedo, so it's been removed and its connectors taped off — the bike currently runs with no speedo. Already disassembled it, scraped the corrosion off the boards, and dried it thoroughly. Plan: reassemble and reconnect — but AFTER the power-loss fault is solved, so you're not chasing two variables at once. Reintroduce it last and re-test. The water intrusion here is also a clue: check the neighboring steering-head connectors for the same corrosion.
Recommended after sitting — 10W-40 JASO MA/MA2, ~1.4 qt with filter; filter Suzuki 16510-29F00 / HiFlo HF139 (see maintenance). Pair it with the electrical diagnosis when you're up there.
